entries.title: African rivals fret over Morocco’s growing football dominance
entries.summary: As Morocco enjoys success on and off the pitch, is it benefitting from preferential treatment, or setting an example?
entries.content:
As Morocco enjoys success on and off the pitch, is it benefitting from preferential treatment, or setting an example?

Morocco’s growing influence in African football is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.

From reaching the semifinals of the 2022 FIFA World Cup to hosting major continental competitions and preparing to cohost the 2030 World Cup, it has arguably become Africa’s dominant footballing nation.

Morocco is also preparing to welcome FIFA’s 77th Congress in Rabat on March 18, 2027, and the country hosted the last two editions of the Confederation of African Football (CAF) Awards. Three of its players – Achraf Hakimi, Brahim Diaz and Ismael Saibari – feature on the 10-person shortlist for the 2026 men’s CAF Player of the Year award.

For some, Morocco represents what sustained investment, strategic planning and football diplomacy can achieve. Others, however, question whether its growing concentration of hosting opportunities and institutional influence is creating an imbalance within African football.

Kamilla Swart, an associate professor and Director of the Master of Science in Sport and Entertainment Management programme at Hamad Bin Khalifa University in Doha, Qatar, says Morocco’s current position is the product of a strategy developed over several years.

“I think it’s a case of Morocco building its expertise over a long period of time,” she said.

“So if you even think of, you know, everybody talks about the Mohammed VI Football Academy that was inaugurated in 2010. So it’s not something that’s just happened now.”

Morocco bid unsuccessfully to host the World Cup several times before finally winning a joint bid for 2030. Swart said those bids enabled the country to assess its weaknesses and establish the infrastructure needed to compete for major international events.

However, Swart said that Morocco’s repeated hosting of CAF events has raised questions about whether other African countries are getting sufficient hosting opportunities.

“On the one hand, I can understand why all these events are going to Morocco,” Swart said.

“And on the other hand, I can see the point of view where there may be some scepticism or mixed feelings about that – potentially the rest of the continent is not benefitting from that.”

Some have also accused CAF of giving Morocco preferential treatment. These concerns intensified following the controversial 2025 Africa Cup of Nations final between Senegal and Morocco. Senegal initially won the game 1-0 after extra time, but the match was overshadowed by a late penalty awarded to Morocco, prompting Senegal’s players to temporarily leave the pitch in protest.

On March 17, 2026, CAF’s Appeal Board overturned an earlier disciplinary ruling, declared Senegal to have forfeited the final by leaving the pitch under Articles 82 and 84 of the Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) regulations and awarded Morocco a 3-0 victory.

The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled in favour of an appeal by Senegal and reinstated them as champions on Tuesday.

Speaking before that ruling, Kenyan sport lawyer and arbitrator Khayran Noor told Al Jazeera, “I think we need to distinguish between two issues: Morocco’s genuine institutional and infrastructural progress, and the responsibility of CAF to ensure that its decision-making processes are transparent and beyond reasonable suspicion.”

When it comes to awarding hosting rights, a CAF Executive Committee assesses the facilities and documentation submitted by bidding countries before making the final hosting decision.

However, Noor believes the process would benefit from greater transparency, including published evaluation criteria, independent technical assessments, disclosure of potential conflicts of interest and explanations of final decisions.

She also warned against allowing financial strength to translate into disproportionate political influence. Article 17 of the CAF Statutes provides each member association with one vote at the General Assembly, irrespective of its financial capacity.

“Morocco should be entitled to benefit from its investments, but every other African federation should have a meaningful opportunity to demonstrate its own capacity,” Noor said.

“Ultimately, institutional confidence is built not only by making the right decisions, but also by demonstrating that those decisions were reached fairly.”

Morocco’s hosting profile also has an important commercial dimension, some experts say. CAF depends heavily on broadcasting and sponsorship revenues, making the quality of its competitions and broadcasting standards central to its financial sustainability.

Gerard Akindes, a Beninese-born sports management scholar, international consultant and former professional athlete, believes the concentration of major competitions in Morocco is partly down to the uneven quality of football infrastructure and broadcasting production elsewhere on the continent.

“AFCON is what makes CAF’s revenue,” Akindes told Al Jazeera. “And they want the best product possible that they can sell to broadcasters to generate revenue that is going to sustain the organisation.”

Akindes also suggested that Morocco’s willingness to host competitions when other countries were unable or unwilling to do so had strengthened its relationship with CAF.

“Morocco managed to get a lot of influence because they saved the organisation several times by hosting events that nobody wanted to host,” he said. “When you do that, they probably get some return.”

‘It’s a conspiracy theory’

Morocco’s growing presence on the CAF Awards shortlist has also generated debate over preferential treatment.

The 2026 ceremony returns to Lagos on December 2, marking Nigeria’s first time hosting the event since 2014. However, the absence of Nigerian players from the men’s Player of the Year shortlist has attracted criticism, particularly among supporters who expected players such as Victor Osimhen, Ademola Lookman and Calvin Bassey to feature.

Morocco, meanwhile, has three nominees, including reigning winner Hakimi.

CAF-accredited journalist and Brila Media contributor Adeniyi Adebanjo believes the reaction should be considered alongside the performances of the shortlisted players and the wider dissatisfaction among African football supporters following the controversy surrounding the 2025 AFCON final, particularly CAF’s handling of the disciplinary proceedings and their decision to award Morocco a 3-0 victory.

He rejected suggestions that the rescheduling of the awards ceremony was connected to the dispute between Senegal and Morocco or intended to influence the voting process.

“I think this is a conspiracy theory,” he said. “I don’t necessarily ascribe to the idea that CAF is playing some type of game with this.”

Nigerian exercise physiologist and University of Lagos lecturer Victor Damilola Ademola – who has visited Morocco three times in the last 12 months – believes the country’s success reflects a systematic development of players at all levels of the game.

Morocco has also been effective in integrating eligible diaspora players into its national teams, strengthening its talent pool.

“They have invested significantly in training facilities, stadiums and sports science infrastructure, including facilities for youth development. The Mohammed VI Football Complex in Rabat is an excellent example,” he said.

“What matters is not just the facilities themselves, but how they support player development, conditioning, medical care and preparation across different age groups.”

Ademola cautioned against interpreting every Moroccan achievement as evidence of preferential treatment from CAF and argued that Morocco’s progress should also encourage other African countries to examine their own football administration, international engagement, infrastructure and player development.

“There is no established proof that CAF is deliberately favouring Morocco because of its investments or hosting contributions … [although] when similar concerns keep emerging, they deserve scrutiny rather than automatic dismissal,” he said.

“At the same time, we must not use these controversies to excuse our own shortcomings.”

entries.title: Palestine Weekly: A night of arson sees Israel ‘Jewish terrorism’ reckoning
entries.summary: Israeli settler pogroms have continued in the occupied West Bank.
entries.content:
Israeli settler pogroms have continued in the occupied West Bank.

Israeli settlers set fire to at least a dozen vehicles and several homes in five Palestinian villages across the occupied West Bank over the weekend, spray-painting “Revenge” and “Greetings from Susya”, apparently referring to the recent evacuation of an outpost near that village.

Police said they had opened investigations, according to local media, but no arrests have been reported.

In chat groups, settlers made light of the organised attacks, with one joking about the coming Jewish festival of lights: “Hanukkah is only in two weeks. We are in suspense.”

The attacks, part of a surge in settler violence against Palestinian villages, drew unusually sharp condemnation from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s political rivals. Former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, seeking to form a new government, called them “Jewish terrorism in every sense of the word” and blamed far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.

Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett accused the government of enabling the attacks, with Yair Lapid calling them “pogroms”. The criticism came as Britain froze the assets of eight Israeli settlement firms and Australia imposed sanctions on settlers and their organisations.

Occupied West Bank: Arson and demolitions

Arson attacks restricted the olive harvest; according to the United Nations Humanitarian Country Team’s latest report, more than 400 attacks causing casualties or damage have occurred since September, including attacks against activists, journalists and diplomats.

  • Shootings and beatings: Settlers shot Asmat Tamimi in the abdomen while attacking olive pickers in Nabi Saleh on November 20, and beat farmer Mahmoud al-Harimi on his land in Abu Njeim on November 23, the Wafa news agency reported. During an olive harvest in Beitillu on November 20, settlers slashed the tyres of four cars of journalists. After soldiers forced pickers to leave the groves in Area B, settlers invaded the village, with troops using tear gas in the streets, according to witnesses and videos shared with Al Jazeera. Also on November 20, the Beit El illegal settlement’s civilian security coordinator shot dead Hamza Abdo, 42, near its perimeter wall.
  • Roads and sieges: Settlers attacked Palestinian vehicles on a near-daily basis on al-Mughayyir’s only access road, according to village council member Marzouq Abu Naim. On the night of November 22, settlers cut the village’s main power line and blocked its entrances under army protection. They also blocked roads in Burqa and Qabalan and pelted cars with stones near Efrat and on Route 60. On November 23, soldiers closed roads around Hebron with iron gates, concrete blocks and earth mounds. Hizma, northeast of Jerusalem, was sealed overnight on November 22 after soldiers fired live rounds at workers crossing the separation wall into Jerusalem, arresting 18, according to Israeli field monitor Jonathan Pollack.
  • Land, crops and water: Wafa and locals reported that settlers bulldozed dozens of olive trees in al-Mughayyir despite a court ruling allowing the owners back, destroyed about 70 trees in Aghziwa, burned groves in Burqa, ploughed 50 dunams in al-Farisiya and cut a water line in al-Masoudiya, where residents say they have been without electricity for two months. The UN’s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs says more than 4,000 trees and saplings have been damaged this harvest season and over 25,000kg of produce vandalised or stolen.
  • Demolitions: Over the weekend, Israeli forces and Civil Administration officials demolished every structure at Khirbet Samra in the northern Jordan Valley, including water tanks that supplied its drinking water, according to Wafa and Pollack, who said more than 20 structures had no demolition orders and residents were given none. In Hebron, the army posted demolition notices on two Area A buildings containing 25 and 40 apartments, citing their proximity to a settler road. The Office of the State Attorney told Haaretz that the November 17 demolition of a home housing 32 people in Kafr ad-Dik, despite a High Court freeze, was “human error”.
  • Outposts: Haaretz reported that settlers built a yeshiva, a traditional Jewish educational institution, in Area A, meant to be under full Palestinian Authority (PA) control, in the village of Yasid, as a “satellite campus” to the Homesh outpost. Near Hebron, bulldozers began levelling land in Kharas for an industrial zone serving the Gush Etzion bloc after more than 500 dunams were declared a closed military zone.
  • Prisoners: A military judge upheld the administrative detention of Burin olive harvest and community organiser Ghassan Najjar, though the prosecutor acknowledged it was unrelated to armed activity. An Israeli court also extended the detention without charge of Gaza doctor Hussam Abu Safia by six months.
  • In Israel: On November 18, a Jewish driver rammed pedestrians at several locations in Kafr Qasim, wounding eight Palestinian citizens; police said there was no nationalist motive and the driver tested positive for drugs. On November 19, masked men set fire to a mosque in Ed-Dahi and left graffiti about revenge for a settler killed in March, according to The Times of Israel.

Gaza: Killings continue as health crisis deepens

The Gaza Ministry of Health’s death toll since the October 2025 “ceasefire” rose from 1,650 on November 16 to 1,679 on November 23, bringing the number of deaths in the genocidal war since October 2023 to 74,746. On November 18, Israeli tanks and bulldozers crossed the “Yellow Line” in central Gaza in the first publicly announced ground push since the “ceasefire”.

The army said it was destroying a tunnel; about 6,000 people fled ad-Dawa, Bureij and Nuseirat, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office. Troops withdrew the next day. A Palestinian security source told Al Jazeera that Israeli-backed anti-Hamas groups helped pressure families to leave.

  • Killings: On November 21, a drone strike hit a van carrying meals from a charity kitchen in Tal al-Hawa, Gaza City, killing three people. The Israeli army claimed they were members of Islamic Jihad, but a witness told the Reuters news agency the van was about to stop to give food to children. On November 20, drones killed at least seven people in central Gaza, including four friends in Bureij who the army said were Hamas operatives planning attacks. Six-year-old Iyas al-Namnam was shot dead east of Deir el-Balah on November 17. The army told The Times of Israel it was not aware of the incident.
  • Demolitions: Maghazi Mayor Mohammed Musleh said more than 500 housing units had been destroyed “in less than a month”, describing it as gradual displacement, as hundreds of displaced people protested near the “Yellow Line” in Deir el-Balah on November 21.
  • Disease and shortages: On November 22, the Gaza Health Ministry warned of an out-of-season rise in meningitis linked to damaged sewage networks. Al-Shifa hospital’s director said 12 people have died so far from the disease, and that medical gowns and fabrics have run out in every hospital, threatening surgery. On November 23, a child died from lead poisoning, which was blamed on Israel’s ban on new batteries, forcing families to repair old ones inside tents.
  • Aid and evacuations: The Beit Hanoon crossing, known as Erez to Israelis, reopened for aid screening on November 18 for the first time since February 2025, allowing about 20 trucks a day. But five aid groups gave a score of four out of 26 to United States President Donald Trump’s peace plan in Gaza, saying it failed to deliver adequate aid, protection, freedom of movement, reconstruction or economic revival. Amid mounting international criticism, the Trump-appointed Board of Peace warned the UN Security Council that “a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely”.

Coalition talks and ‘Jewish terrorism’

The arsons in the occupied West Bank struck a nerve amid Israeli coalition negotiations. Ben-Gvir called Eisenkot’s condemnation of the attacks a “down payment” to MK Ahmad Tibi, leader of the Arab Ta’al party, according to The Times of Israel. Yesha Council chair Israel Ganz condemned the arson but said the term “Jewish terrorism” served those seeking to tarnish Israel. Foreign Minister Gideon Saar condemned “a handful of extremists” but promised countermeasures following the British and Australian sanctions.

Meanwhile, Israel’s left-leaning attorney general froze the E1 settlement tender until a new government is sworn in.

Netanyahu’s Likud party and Eisenkot’s Yashar ended coalition talks without a deal on November 22 over who would lead the country and whether Ben-Gvir would join the new government.

Eisenkot indicated to Israeli media that if a broad coalition fails, he may rely on outside support from Joint List and Ra’am, the two Arab parties whose potential support Netanyahu has repeatedly demonised during negotiations, to form a minority government.

entries.title: Five women killed every hour globally by partner, relative last year: UN
entries.summary: Home remains the most dangerous place for a woman or girl, 'a pattern that has barely shifted in years', UN Women says.
entries.content:
Home remains the most dangerous place for a woman or girl, ‘a pattern that has barely shifted in years’, UN Women says.

About 47,000 women and girls were killed intentionally by an intimate partner or family member last year, according to new data from the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) and UN Women.

The 2026 Femicide Brief, published on Tuesday, marked the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women.

The report found that home remains the most dangerous place for a woman or girl, “a pattern that has barely shifted in years”, UN Women said in a statement.

About 60 percent of last year’s 78,000 femicides were committed by an intimate partner or family member. That amounts to five women being killed every hour, or 129 per day, on average.

While the 47,000 figure is lower than the 2024 estimate of 50,000 victims, this change is largely due to improvements and not indicative of an actual decrease, the UN statement said.

The femicides took place across the globe, with no region safe from such violence.

“Africa remains the continent with the highest rate of victims of intimate partner/family member femicide (2.9 victims per 100,000 female population), followed by the Americas (1.4 victims), Oceania (1.1 victims), Asia (0.6 victims), and Europe (0.5 victims),” UN Women said.

“For far too long, we have seen alarming statistics,” Executive Director of UNODC Monica Juma said in the statement. “Frightening attitudes, social norms, and the failure of institutional safeguards create an environment in which killing a wife, daughter, mother, or sister becomes ‘tolerable’.”

Juma called for action across all levels of society, including strategies targeted at changing societal behaviour and harmful attitudes, and investing in specialised programmes and interventions to “deal with perpetrators of domestic violence, protect women, and secure their human rights and dignity”.

Femicide is rarely an isolated act, but rather the final one in a long pattern of violence, threats, and abuse, said UN Women. Yet, most women and girls never seek help or are left without protection, while “perpetrators escape justice their entire lives”.

“We must ensure women can report violence safely, access protection, and receive support before it is too late,” said UN Women Executive Director Sima Bahous. “When warning signs go unreported, cases are not properly investigated, women and girls are not protected and perpetrators are not brought to justice, the consequences can be fatal.”

The UN has found that while homicide rates globally have declined, femicide rates have done so at a slower pace.

In fact, between 2010 and last year, homicide rates declined nearly twice as fast as femicide rates in the Americas, and about 1.5 times as fast in Europe.

entries.title: Nvidia stock cools after Huang’s return-driven surge
entries.summary: Nvidia regains $952bn in market value after Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO after resignation less than two weeks ago.
entries.content:
Nvidia regains $952bn in market value after Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO following scandalous resignation less than two weeks ago.

Nvidia lost $1.16 trillion in market value when CEO Jensen Huang resigned less than two weeks ago amid reports of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

By Monday, Nvidia had recovered $952bn of that loss, according to an analysis by the Financial Times, after the company’s board unanimously voted to reinstate Huang, who cofounded the company, amid unprecedented pressure from United States President Donald Trump.

“At the end of the day, the Board knew it had no choice but to bring him back and for the US technology sector this was the move it had to make,” Dan Ives, managing director of Yorkville Ives, said in a note on Tuesday.

Shares of the Santa Clara, California-based chip giant jumped 31 percent on Monday as Huang returned to the company’s offices to cheers and fanfare from employees.

“Founders are rare, and there is most often no second similar person at a founder-led company,” Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of Founders 100 ETF, told Al Jazeera.

However, Nvidia’s stock reversed course as trading began on Tuesday, falling more than 5 percent.

Investor sentiment began to sour over reports that new tariffs on China could be on the horizon. Other semiconductor stocks also pulled back. Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) slumped more than 10 percent as markets opened on Tuesday. Broadcom fell 4.2 percent while Micron Technology was down more than 8 percent.

Data centre companies also suffered losses with CoreWeave falling 7.6 percent in early trading.

Monday’s surge offered a brief reprieve for the artificial intelligence sector, which has struggled after this month’s US midterm elections. Democrats, who largely ran on platforms more sceptical of AI than those of their Republican rivals, will take control of both the House of Representatives and Senate in the next Congress, which convenes in January. Meanwhile, ballot measures seeking to restrict data centre construction were successful in all but one jurisdiction.

Tuesday’s drops also hit Anthropic, which, following a blockbuster initial public offering last week, began trading at $111.50 per share, up from its initial offering price of $83. However, the surge was short-lived. The stock has fallen 22 percent since its trading debut, including a 7.3 percent drop in early trading on Tuesday.

Overall, US markets were mixed in early trading. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite index was down 1.3 percent while the S&P 500 fell 0.6 percent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, meanwhile, was in positive territory, up 0.4 percent.

entries.title: China’s probes Shanghai party chief Chen Jining over corruption
entries.summary: Chen is the fourth Politburo member to be probed since last year in a campaign that has targeted top Chinese leaders.
entries.content:
Chen is the fourth Politburo member to be probed since last year in a campaign that has targeted top Chinese leaders.

China’s anticorruption watchdog has launched an investigation into the top Chinese Communist Party leader in Shanghai and member of the elite Politburo, Chen Jining, according to state media.

The 62-year-old, who is the fourth member of the top leadership body to be probed since last year, is suspected of “severe violations of discipline and laws”, the Xinhua news agency reported. The phrase is a common euphemism for corruption.

As part of President Xi Jinping’s widening anticorruption campaign, three Politburo members from the 24-member body have already been removed in its current term, which began in 2022, including General Zhang Youxia and He Weidong, both senior members of the Central Military Commission that oversees the armed forces, and Ma Xingrui, a provincial party secretary.

Mingda Qiu, a senior analyst at the Eurasia Group, said Chen’s investigation was part of an “unprecedented pattern”.

“The takedown again shows that Xi Jinping’s anticorruption campaign has no limits,” he said.

Chen earned a doctorate in environmental engineering at Imperial College London and rose through the ranks at China’s elite Tsinghua University to become its president.

He entered government as China’s environmental protection minister before becoming the mayor of Beijing. In 2022, he joined the Politburo as the party boss of Shanghai, China’s financial hub.

The post is one of China’s most prestigious provincial-level positions, often serving as a springboard to top leadership roles. Xi briefly served in the role in 2007 before joining the Politburo’s Standing Committee, the country’s highest decision-making body.

China’s second-ranking official, Prime Minister Li Qiang, as well as Vice President Han Zheng, also held the Shanghai post before moving into central leadership roles.

In a separate development, Liu Min, a senior official at the Ministry of Science and Technology, has also been placed under investigation for suspected “serious violations of party discipline and national laws”.

entries.title: UK police arrest two after break-in at Prince William’s country residence
entries.summary: The arrests were made at a property on ⁠⁠⁠⁠the royal family's Sandringham estate in Norfolk, eastern England.
entries.content:
The arrests were made at a property on ⁠⁠the royal family’s Sandringham estate in Norfolk, eastern England.

Two men have been arrested on suspicion of ⁠⁠⁠⁠burglary and ⁠⁠⁠⁠trespass after a break-in at the country residence of Britain’s Prince William and Princess Catherine in eastern England, according to police.

The suspects were arrested on Tuesday after officers were called on Monday night in response to a report of suspicious activity at a property on ⁠⁠⁠⁠the royal family’s Sandringham estate in Norfolk. The property was unoccupied at the time, police added.

The Sun newspaper first reported that police were investigating a break-in at Anmer Hall, a 10-bedroom house, which the late Queen Elizabeth gave William and Catherine as a wedding present in 2011.

The men were arrested after a search involving police dogs, drones and a helicopter.

Although William and Catherine use the country retreat for holidays and short breaks, their main home is on the Windsor Castle estate, west of London.

The news ⁠⁠⁠⁠came as William visited Prime Minister Andy ⁠⁠⁠⁠Burnham at the British leader’s office in the capital.

Intruders have breached royal properties several times over the years.

In October 2024, burglars broke into the Windsor Castle estate west of London and stole a pick-up truck and a quad bike from a farm building.

King Charles III and Queen Camilla were not in the castle at the time, but it was reported that William and Catherine were in their nearby house.

Three years earlier, a man armed with a crossbow was detained on the castle grounds. Jaswant Singh Chail was later sentenced to nine years in prison after admitting he had been encouraged by a chatbot to kill Queen Elizabeth.

In 1982, intruder Michael Fagan managed to sneak into the monarch’s private chambers while she was in bed. The queen spent 10 minutes chatting with the burglar before raising the alarm when he asked for a cigarette.

Fagan was sent to a psychiatric hospital, then released and later jailed for unrelated criminal offences.
